how-much-to-charge-to-paint-kitchen-cabi.text:
← Cabinet refinishing bid calculator

How much to charge to paint kitchen cabinets

The number a homeowner wants is a price per door. That number is not a takeoff. A 10-door galley with eight drawer fronts, a greasy range wall, and a dark-to-light extra coat is not the same job as ten shop-sprayed doors with the existing pulls left on. The door count is identical. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count drawer fronts and face frames, not just doors

A typical galley has almost as many drawer fronts as doors, and every opening still has a face frame that stays on the wall. Interior painting prices walls by the square foot. Cabinet refinishing prices millwork by the piece. Quoting both from a published per-door number is how the boxes and the drawers eat the door margin.

Hardware and degrease are hours, not a rounded extra

Two hinges per door plus a pull on every door and drawer is 30–40 pieces on a small kitchen. Each one is remove, bag, and rehang. Degrease on a cooking wall is a half-day before primer will stick. Those hours do not appear in a per-door special written for a clean laundry-room cabinet.

Shop spray, on-site spray, and brush are different jobs

Doors off in a booth is the fastest finish. On-site spray adds containment and masking. Brush and roll is slower still. The calculator keeps a finish labor factor on the painted pieces only — hardware bag-and-rehang and degrease stay the same. Mixing the two hides which part of a high bid is booth time and which part is grease.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $38/h finisher loaded at 30% payroll burden is $49.40. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. On the sample 10-door / 8-drawer galley the calculator prices about $3,390 ($339 per door, $126 per painted piece, 32.8 crew-hours, walk-away $2,542). The same kitchen as on-site brush with a dark-to-light extra coat is several hundred dollars more. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a paint specification, an adhesion warranty, a permit, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Finish system, sanding grit, and whether the boxes get sprayed in place are yours to confirm.

Price your kitchen

Common questions

How much to charge to paint kitchen cabinets?

Charge from doors, drawer fronts, face-frame openings, hardware remove-and-rehang, degrease, finish method, extra coats for a color change, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 10-door / 8-drawer galley on shop spray prices around $3,390 on the sample rates in this calculator — about $339 per door, or $126 per painted piece.

Why is a per-door cabinet quote dangerous?

Homeowners count doors. Drawer fronts, face frames, hardware, degrease, and a dark-to-light extra coat do not scale with that count. Matching a cheaper per-door quote written for a shop-sprayed same-color job is how an on-site brush kitchen becomes a loss.

How much extra should I charge to go from dark cabinets to a light color?

Treat it as an extra finish coat on every removable piece — doors and drawer fronts — not a blended add-on to the door count. On the sample rates that is about 0.22 hours per removable piece. Face frames usually need the extra coat too; fold that into opening hours if your crew sprays boxes in place.

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not painting, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

Bid the doors, the drawers, and the degrease — not the door count.

A flat per-door quote treats a 10-door galley with eight drawer fronts, a greasy range wall, and a dark-to-light extra coat as the same job as ten shop-sprayed doors. Drawer fronts, face frames, hardware remove-and-rehang, and an extra coat do not scale with the door count the homeowner counts. Price those extras separately, then see the walk-away number.

Where the cost goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and coverage are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a paint specification — replace them with your own takeoff.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    What does this refinishing estimate include?

    The price adds up door, drawer-front, and face-frame labor scaled by your finish method, hardware remove-and-rehang (or replacement) labor, degrease and prep hours, an extra finish coat when the color change calls for one, primer and finish material by the gallon, sandpaper and containment supplies, and new hardware when checked — plus travel and equipment, overhead, and your target margin, all from the piece counts and rates you enter, not a flat price-per-door list.

    Why does a face-frame opening cost less than a door of the same size?

    A face-frame opening is painted in place, not pulled, sanded on a bench, and sprayed in a booth, so it counts as 0.6 of a piece — not a full door — when the calculator sizes primer and finish gallons. Doors and drawer fronts, which are removed and finished off the cabinet, each count as a full piece.

    Why does on-site brush work cost so much more than shop spray for the same door count?

    Each finish method has its own labor factor: shop spray (doors off, in a booth) is the baseline, on-site spray in containment runs 28% more hours on the same doors, and on-site brush or roll runs 55% more — masking, multiple thin coats, and working around a kitchen the crew cannot fully close off all cost time that a booth does not. Switching finish method rescales door, drawer, and opening hours; it does not touch hardware or degrease hours, which take the same time regardless of how the piece gets its coats.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your piece counts, wages, costs, or prices. Only your business details for the printed proposal are kept in this browser’s local storage so you do not retype them, and the customer’s details are never saved.

    What’s the difference between the refinish price and the walk-away price?

    The refinish price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — doors, drawers, openings, hardware, primer, and finish — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all.

    Does this check paint adhesion or substrate condition?

    No. Hours, coverage, and material rates are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not a paint specification or a guarantee of adhesion. Whether a particular cabinet substrate needs extra degrease, deglossing, or a bonding primer beyond what you have entered is still a judgment call from the site walk — this tool prices the finish system you choose, it does not test it.

vs-a-flat-price-per-door.html.text:
← Cabinet Refinishing Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per door

“$339 a door” is not a price for a cabinet refinish — it is a price for one specific door count, drawer ratio, finish method, and color change, quietly applied to every kitchen that calls in.

What a flat price per door is

A flat price per door is the fastest way to quote: multiply the door count by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kitchen — a shop-sprayed galley, one finish color, existing hardware reinstalled — and then reused for every kitchen afterward, whether or not the next job carries the same drawer fronts, hardware, finish method, and color change.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the doors, drawer fronts, face-frame openings, and hardware pieces, the finish method (shop spray, on-site spray, or brush), the color change, degrease hours, and whether hardware is replaced, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices doors, drawer fronts, face frames, and hardware separately, scales labor by finish method and extra coats, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this kitchen, not a generic one.

What a flat price per door doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate per door whether the kitchen has 8 drawer fronts or 24, even though drawer fronts and face-frame openings do not scale with the door count a homeowner counts. Prices doors, drawer fronts, and face-frame openings as separate piece counts, so a kitchen with more drawers than doors is never quoted off a door-only rate.
Has no line for hardware remove-and-rehang, or for replacing hardware with new pulls and knobs on every piece. Prices hardware labor per piece, and adds material cost per piece when hardware is replaced, so a kitchen swapping 114 pulls and knobs costs more than one reinstalling the originals.
Applies one rate regardless of finish method, even though on-site spray runs 28% more labor hours than a shop-spray booth on the same doors, and on-site brush runs 55% more. Scales door, drawer, and opening hours by the finish method's own labor factor, so on-site brush work costs more than the same doors sprayed off-site in a booth.
Prices a dark-to-light color change the same as touching up the same family of color, even though dark-to-light needs a whole extra finish coat on every removable piece. Adds extra-coat hours on doors and drawer fronts when the color change calls for one, so a dark-to-light kitchen is never quoted at the same-color rate.
Gives the painter a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat per-door rate would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two kitchens, the same door-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets:

JobThis calculator's priceA flat $339.00/door rate, applied by door count aloneGap
10-door, 8-drawer galley, shop spray, same-family color, existing hardware reinstalled (the job this flat rate was built on)$3,389.95 — $339.00/door$3,389.95 (same job, same rate)No gap: this is the one job the flat rate fits.
30-door, 24-drawer, 26-opening kitchen, on-site brush, dark-to-light extra coat, 114 pieces of new hardware$13,683.76 bid price; $10,262.82 break-even cost$10,169.85The flat rate quotes $92.97 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $3,513.91 below the calculator's bid price.

Both flat-rate quotes use the $339.00/door rate the 10-door galley's own price works out to. Applied to the 30-door kitchen's door count, that rate carries none of the on-site brush labor factor, the dark-to-light extra coat, the 16 extra drawer fronts and 17 extra openings, or the $912 of new hardware the bigger job actually needs — and it prices below what the job costs to complete. Run your own kitchen's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one kitchen it was built for, and nothing about a per-door number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per door get a cabinet refinishing quote wrong?

Because the cost driver is drawer fronts, face frames, hardware, finish method, and color change, not door count. A 30-door kitchen with 24 drawer fronts, on-site brush finishing, new hardware on 114 pieces, and a dark-to-light extra coat needs far more labor and material per door than a shop-sprayed 10-door galley in one color. A flat per-door rate charges every door the same regardless of what else the job carries.

What does a flat per-door rate usually leave out entirely?

Drawer fronts and face-frame openings, which do not scale with the door count a homeowner counts; hardware remove-and-rehang or replacement; the extra labor factor for on-site spray or brush work versus a shop spray booth; and the extra finish coat a dark-to-light color change needs. A per-door number has no line for any of them.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets: a 10-door, 8-drawer galley, shop-sprayed in one color prices at $3,389.95 -- $339.00 a door. Applying that same $339.00-a-door rate to a 30-door, 24-drawer kitchen with on-site brush finishing, a dark-to-light extra coat, and 114 pieces of new hardware quotes $10,169.85 -- $92.97 below that job's own $10,262.82 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $3,513.91 below the calculator's own $13,683.76 bid price.

Is a flat price per door ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same finish method, same color change, no hardware replacement, a similar drawer-to-door ratio -- a flat per-door rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which kitchen it was built on and neither does the painter until the doors are actually counted.

Does this calculator know what paint or labor costs in my market?

No. It has no data on local paint invoices or labor rates. It takes the door, drawer, opening, and hardware counts, the finish method, color change, and degrease hours, plus the labor hours and material costs you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-door rate skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. Kickserv

Two different shapes: Kickserv is an account-based platform for running a home service company's whole operation, including scheduling the crew and invoicing the customer once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this kitchen's refinish cost, before you offer it.

What each tool is for

Kickserv, founded in 2006, is a field service management platform used by home service businesses — painting, cleaning, HVAC, plumbing and general contracting among them — to run client and job management, online estimates and invoicing, scheduling and crew dispatch, and online payments, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Kickserv's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of field service software describe scheduling, invoicing and collecting payment for a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a cabinet refinish should cost from door and drawer counts, hardware, finish method and degrease before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Kickserv does. It does not manage a client list, dispatch a crew across a season, or collect a payment. It takes one kitchen — doors, drawer fronts, face-frame openings, hardware pieces, finish method (shop spray, on-site spray, or brush), color change, and degrease hours — plus loaded crew wage, payroll burden, primer and finish material, supplies, travel and equipment, overhead and target margin, and turns that into the refinish price, the price per door, the price per painted piece, the effective crew hourly rate and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears your own break-even floor, and a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Should I use this calculator or Kickserv?

They do different jobs, and a cabinet-painting business of any size will likely end up touching both.
